content: Bifocals are eyeglasses that incorporate lenses with two distinct optical powers within each lens. They are most commonly prescribed for individuals with presbyopia who also require vision correction for myopia, hypermetropia, and/or astigmatism. Benjamin Franklin is widely credited with inventing the first pair of bifocals in the early 1760s. The earliest evidence of his double spectacles appears in a political cartoon from 1764. Numerous letters and publications from that era reference Dr. Franklin's invention, including his own mention of them in a letter dated August 21, 1784. The term bifocals was later coined in 1824 by John Isaac Hawkins, the inventor of trifocals, who also credited Franklin with their creation. Franklin's original bifocals were constructed by placing the most convex lenses, designed for close-up viewing, in the lower half of the frame, while the least convex lenses were positioned in the upper half. Until the early 20th century, bifocals were made by cutting two separate lenses in half and combining them within a single frame. This method often resulted in fragile spectacles and various complications. A technique for fusing the lens sections together was developed by Louis de Wecker in the late 19th century and patented by Dr. John L. Borsch, Jr. in 1908. Modern bifocals are typically manufactured by molding a reading segment into a primary lens, and they are available in various shapes and sizes, such as the straight-top or D-segment design, which is 28 mm wide. These are widely accessible through most eye care providers. The division of the visual field in bifocals can cause headaches and dizziness in some users. Adjusting to the limited field of view provided by the reading segment often requires time, as users must learn to move their head or the reading material rather than their eyes. Additionally, computer monitors, which are usually positioned directly in front of users, can lead to muscle fatigue due to the unusual head angles and constant movement required. This issue can be alleviated by using trifocal lenses. Ongoing research aims to address the limited field of vision inherent in current bifocal designs. Advances in materials and technologies may enable lenses with adjustable optical power. Researchers at the University of Arizona have developed a switchable lens using a liquid crystal layer sandwiched between two glass substrates. When electricity is applied, the effective refractive index changes, allowing the optical power of the lens to be varied.
